claims.text: Position: the left kidney is at about T12–L3; the right sits lower because the liver displaces it.
claims.quote: The left kidney is located at about the T12 to L3 vertebrae, whereas the right is lower due to slight displacement by the liver.

claims.text: Blood flow: about 25 percent of resting cardiac output.
claims.quote: The kidneys are well vascularized, receiving about 25 percent of the cardiac output at rest.

claims.text: Adrenal gland: sits on the superior aspect of each kidney.
claims.quote: On the superior aspect of each kidney is the adrenal gland.

claims.text: Inside: an outer renal cortex and an inner medulla.
claims.quote: A frontal section through the kidney reveals an outer region called the renal cortex and an inner region called the medulla

claims.text: Hilum: the entry and exit for the kidney's vessels, nerves, lymphatics and ureter.
claims.quote: The renal hilum is the entry and exit site for structures servicing the kidneys: vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and ureters.

claims.text: Renal pelvis: formed from the calyces; its smooth muscle moves urine into the ureter by peristalsis.
claims.quote: Emerging from the hilum is the renal pelvis, which is formed from the major and minor calyxes in the kidney. The smooth muscle in the renal pelvis funnels urine via peristalsis into the ureter.

claims.text: Renal veins: normally the largest veins entering the inferior vena cava.
claims.quote: Blood supply from the kidneys flows into each renal vein, normally the largest veins entering the inferior vena cava.

claims.text: Renal artery: a branch of the abdominal aorta that supplies each kidney.
claims.quote: Renal artery Branch of the abdominal aorta; supplies each kidney
claims.locator: Table: Vessels of the Abdominal Aorta

claims.text: Retroperitoneal: the kidneys and ureters completely; the bladder has peritoneum only over its dome.
claims.quote: The kidneys and ureters are completely retroperitoneal, and the bladder has a peritoneal covering only over the dome.
The ureters are approximately 30 cm long.

claims.text: Trigone: the triangle at the bladder base between the two ureteral openings and the urethra.
claims.quote: The urethra in both males and females begins inferior and central to the two ureteral openings forming the three points of a triangular-shaped area at the base of the bladder called the trigone

claims.text: Detrusor: parasympathetic outflow contracts it and relaxes the internal urethral sphincter.
claims.quote: The resulting parasympathetic neural outflow causes contraction of the detrusor muscle and relaxation of the involuntary internal urethral sphincter.

claims.text: External sphincter: voluntary control through the pudendal nerve (S2–S4).
claims.quote: Voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter is a function of the pudendal nerve. It arises in the sacral region of the spinal cord, traveling via the S2–S4 nerves of the sacral plexus.

claims.text: Female urethra: about 4 cm; its short length is the best explanation for more UTIs in females.
claims.quote: Its short length, about 4 cm, is less of a barrier to fecal bacteria than the longer male urethra and the best explanation for the greater incidence of UTI in females.

claims.text: Male urethra: averages 20 cm; it passes through the prostate and has four regions (preprostatic, prostatic, membranous, spongy/penile).
claims.quote: The male urethra passes through the prostate gland immediately inferior to the bladder before passing below the pubic symphysis (see Figure 25.3b). The length of the male urethra varies between people but averages 20 cm in length. It is divided into four regions: the preprostatic urethra, the prostatic urethra, the membranous urethra, and the spongy or penile urethra.
